tagline: Neon signs trace earlier Las Vegas along a former highway.
intro: Las Vegas Boulevard’s downtown byway passes older motels, wedding chapels and the casino district at Fremont Street. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway at 3.41 miles and allows 15 minutes for the drive. It singles out the concentration of neon sign art, including original and restored signs from the 1950s. Nevada’s transportation department emphasizes the mix of historic and modern architecture. FHWA calls the roadway a work of art at night, crediting the neon advertising for wedding chapels, motels, museums and other cultural attractions.

The boulevard formerly carried US 91, the main highway between Los Angeles and Salt Lake City, before Interstate 15 bypassed it. In 1996 the Neon Museum began reinstalling old signs downtown to attract visitors. National byway designation followed in 2009, accompanied by more vintage signs along the street. A neon slipper from the demolished Silver Slipper casino was placed in the median in front of the museum as part of that project.

Travel north from Sahara Avenue, passing The Strat and the stretch of older motels and chapels before reaching downtown’s Fremont Street. Continue to the Neon Museum and the Old Las Vegas Mormon Fort at Washington Avenue. The state-designated downtown corridor ends there.
notice: Original and restored neon signs include examples from the 1950s.

moments.title: The Strat
moments.text: The Strat’s 1,149-foot observation tower began as Bob Stupak’s plan for a giant neon sign at his Vegas World casino. The proposal became a tower with an observation deck and rooftop restaurant. In 1994 he considered raising it to 1,825 feet. The Federal Aviation Administration objected, and the city rejected that height while permitting 1,149 feet. Construction began in 1992, and the tower was topped off in November 1995, before the complex opened the following spring. The complex opened in 1996; the tower now serves as a visual aid for some drivers in the valley.

moments.title: Neon Museum
moments.text: The Neon Museum preserves signs and a piece of roadside architecture: the shell-shaped lobby of the former La Concha Motel. Workers cut the lobby into eight pieces in 2006 and moved it 3.5 miles north along Las Vegas Boulevard. It became the visitor center when the museum opened to the general public in 2012. Young Electric Sign Company’s storage lot supplied fifty signs by 2006. The collection contains more than 200 signs, with hundreds of neon artifacts also held off-site because of limited space. Many unrestored signs need external lighting during night tours.

moments.title: Old Las Vegas Mormon Fort
moments.text: William Bringhurst’s Mormon missionaries chose a site beside a creek flowing from Las Vegas Springs for their fort in 1855. It served as a midpoint on the trail between Salt Lake City and Los Angeles. The missionaries abandoned it with the beginning of the Utah War. Octavius Gass reoccupied it in 1865 and began irrigation works, naming the property Los Vegas Rancho. Ownership changed repeatedly, and the fort came close to destruction several times. The city acquired the fort in 1989 with support from the Daughters of Utah Pioneers; state protection followed in 1991. A visitor center explains this history.
